---
title: "Fair Learning with CKA"
subtitle: "Same probabilistic net, one new term — make the prediction independent of a protected attribute"
---





The [previous note](06-probabilistic-nn-recipe.qmd) turned a network's one number
into a **predictive band**: a Gaussian head $[\mu(x),\ \log\sigma^2(x)]$ trained by
the negative log-likelihood, so the net reports a center $\mu(x)$ *and* the noise it
predicts $\sigma(x)$, with a deep ensemble on top for the ignorance a single net
cannot see.  That recipe is the whole starting point here — we change *nothing* about
it.

This note adds a **new requirement** to that same net.  Sometimes the prediction must
**not depend on a protected attribute** $S$ — sex, race, age — no matter what proxies
the features hide.  State it as a dependence-zero goal:

$$
\operatorname{Dep}\!\big(\mu(x),\ S\big) = 0 .
$$

We already own a bounded dependence measure built for exactly this — **CKA**, the
centered kernel alignment from the [dependence chapter](../dependence/index.qmd), the
same double-centering the distance-correlation ladder used.  There it *measured*
dependence between two return series.  Here it does one new job: turned into a
differentiable penalty, it **constrains** the probabilistic net so its center is
independent of $S$.  The entire recipe is

$$
\underbrace{\operatorname{NLL}\big(y;\ \mu(x),\ \sigma(x)\big)}_{\text{the Note-06 net's loss — head }[\mu,\ \log\sigma^2]}
\;+\;\underbrace{\lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}\!\big(\mu(x),\ S\big)}_{\text{one new term}} .
$$

**What this gives you:** a single extra loss term that makes any probabilistic net's
prediction independent of $S$ — and, because the net is *probabilistic*, the price of
that fairness shows up honestly as a **wider but still-calibrated band**.  When you
forbid the model from using the $S$-signal, accuracy falls; a point net would just be
quietly more wrong, but a net that predicts its own $\sigma(x)$ responds by **widening
the band**, keeping coverage near its nominal $95\%$.  Fairness costs accuracy, and the
probabilistic recipe makes that cost *visible*.

## The Dependence-Zero Goal

A prediction is **fair toward $S$** (in the demographic-parity sense) when knowing
$\mu(x)$ tells you nothing about $S$ — the two are statistically independent.  Dropping
$S$ from the inputs does **not** achieve this: a feature correlated with $S$ — a
**proxy** — lets the network reconstruct it, so the prediction still leans on $S$
through the back door.  We need to *measure* that residual dependence, and to catch the
**nonlinear** part, because a linear check (Pearson) is fooled by a curved leak.

So the new constraint sits entirely on the center $\mu(x)$: we want $\mu(x)$
independent of $S$.  The width $\sigma(x)$ is left free — and that freedom is the
point.  Forced to give up the $S$-signal, the net has two honest moves: shift $\mu$ off
the part of the proxy that carries $S$, and **grow $\sigma$** to admit that it is now
less sure.  The band absorbs the cost.

## Measure the Dependence

CKA is the right instrument because it is **bounded**: $\operatorname{CKA}\in[0,1]$,
reading $0$ when $\mu(x)$ and $S$ are independent and $1$ when one determines the other.
A bounded measure makes the penalty weight $\lambda$ interpretable.  And it is **not a
new measure** — it is the distance-correlation transform with a kernel gram in place of
the distance matrix.  The double-centering is *verbatim* the `centered_distances` step
of the [distance-correlation lab](../dependence/labs/lab-tool1-ladder.qmd): same
$\tilde M_{ij} = M_{ij} - \bar M_{i\cdot} - \bar M_{\cdot j} + \bar M_{\cdot\cdot}$,
only a kernel similarity matrix going in instead of pairwise distances.  Spelled out
with the axes visible, so the shared step is undeniable:

::: {#cka-derivation .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def double_center(M: Float[Array, "n n"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:
    """The dCor transform, verbatim: M̃ᵢⱼ = Mᵢⱼ − M̄ᵢ. − M̄.ⱼ + M̄..

    Identical to `centered_distances` in the distance-correlation lab — only the
    matrix going in differs (a kernel gram here, pairwise distances there).
    """
    row_mean = einx.mean("i j -> i", M)              # M̄ᵢ. — row means
    col_mean = einx.mean("i j -> j", M)              # M̄.ⱼ — column means

    A = einx.subtract("i j, i -> i j", M, row_mean)
    A = einx.subtract("i j, j -> i j", A, col_mean)

    return A + M.mean()                              # add back the grand mean M̄..


def cka_demo(x: Float[Array, "n"], y: Float[Array, "n"]) -> float:
    """CKA = ⟨K̃ₓ, K̃ᵧ⟩ / √(⟨K̃ₓ,K̃ₓ⟩⟨K̃ᵧ,K̃ᵧ⟩) — normalised, double-centred gram alignment."""
    Kx: Float[Array, "n n"] = einx.dot("i, j -> i j", x, x)   # linear gram ⟨xᵢ, xⱼ⟩
    Ky: Float[Array, "n n"] = einx.dot("i, j -> i j", y, y)   # linear gram ⟨yᵢ, yⱼ⟩

    Kxc, Kyc = double_center(Kx), double_center(Ky)  # the SAME centering as dCor
    hsic = lambda A, B: float((A * B).mean())         # ⟨Ã, B̃⟩ — the dependence inner product

    return hsic(Kxc, Kyc) / np.sqrt(hsic(Kxc, Kxc) * hsic(Kyc, Kyc))
```
:::


That is the *linear* CKA.  The penalty we train with uses an **RBF** kernel — the same
kernel the distance ladder used to see curves — so it catches a nonlinear leak a linear
check misses.  The library's `cka_rbf` is that version; it reads $0$ under independence
and $1$ under a deterministic link, and our hand-rolled linear `cka_demo` matches the
library's `cka_linear` exactly:

::: {#cka-check .cell execution_count=4}
``` {.python .cell-code}
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
u: Float[Array, "n"] = rng.standard_normal(400)
v: Float[Array, "n"] = 0.8 * u + 0.4 * rng.standard_normal(400)   # depends on u
w: Float[Array, "n"] = rng.standard_normal(400)                   # independent of u

print(f"hand-rolled cka_demo(u, v) = {cka_demo(u, v):.4f}   (double-centred gram alignment)")
print(f"library  cka_linear(u, v)  = {cka_linear(u, v):.4f}   (identical)")
print(f"library  cka_rbf(u, v)     = {cka_rbf(u, v):.4f}   (dependent → away from 0)")
print(f"library  cka_rbf(u, w)     = {cka_rbf(u, w):.4f}   (independent → near 0)")
```

```
library  cka_rbf(u, v)     = 0.6049   (dependent → away from 0)
```

## The Extended Loss — A Fair Probabilistic Net

Now layer the constraint onto the Note-06 net.  Keep the Gaussian head and its NLL
exactly as they were; add the dependence penalty to the loss:

$$
\mathcal L(\theta)
= \underbrace{-\tfrac1n\sum_i \log\mathcal N\!\big(y_i;\ \mu(x_i),\ \sigma^2(x_i)\big)}_{\text{Note-06 Gaussian NLL — the predictive band}}
\;+\;\lambda\cdot\underbrace{\operatorname{CKA}\!\big(\mu(x),\ S\big)}_{\text{the new fairness term}} .
$$

Fair learning has one rule it never breaks, and it is the whole reason this is honest:
**the sensitive variable $S$ never enters the model — it shapes only the loss.**  The
deployed network takes features alone; $S$ reaches the optimiser through the penalty but
never the inputs.  Three pieces build it:

1. the **Note-06 net** — `Dense(48, tanh) → Dense(48, tanh) → Dense(2)`, the head
   $[\mu,\ \log\sigma^2]$, trained by `gaussian_nll`;
2. the **penalty** $\operatorname{CKA}(\mu, S)$ computed *in-graph* (RBF kernel) so it is
   differentiable — the same `cka_in_graph` the [fairness lab](../fairness/labs/lab-tool2-cka-penalty.qmd) uses;
3. the **total loss** $= \text{Gaussian NLL} + \lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(\mu, S)$,
   added with `add_loss` during training, $S$ arriving as `q` in a `{"x", "q"}` dict.

::: {#fair-prob-net .cell execution_count=5}
``` {.python .cell-code}
def gaussian_nll(y_true, y_pred):
    """−log 𝒩(y; μ, σ²) up to a constant,  head = [μ, log σ²]  (verbatim from Note 06).

    L = ½·(log σ² + (y−μ)²/σ²) — the predictive-band loss; nothing about it changes.
    """
    mu = y_pred[:, :1]                           # μ(x)        [y units]
    log_var = y_pred[:, 1:2]                      # log σ²(x)   [log y² units]

    return ops.mean(0.5 * (log_var + (y_true - mu) ** 2 / ops.exp(log_var)))


def cka_in_graph(pred: Float[Array, "n 1"], s: Float[Array, "n 1"]):
    """RBF CKA(μ, S) in keras.ops so gradients flow — the SAME kernel the fairness lab
    and `keras-fairkl` use, so the penalty here closes the same nonlinear leak."""
    def rbf(z: Float[Array, "n 1"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:
        z = ops.reshape(z, (-1, 1))
        d2 = (z - ops.transpose(z)) ** 2                       # (zᵢ − zⱼ)²   pairwise
        return ops.exp(-d2 / (2.0 * (ops.median(d2) + 1e-12)))  # Kᵢⱼ = exp(−(zᵢ−zⱼ)² / 2σ²)

    def dc(M: Float[Array, "n n"]) -> Float[Array, "n n"]:      # double-centre, in-graph
        return (M - ops.mean(M, 0, keepdims=True)
                  - ops.mean(M, 1, keepdims=True) + ops.mean(M))

    A, B = dc(rbf(pred)), dc(rbf(s))                           # centred RBF grams
    h = lambda P, Q: ops.mean(P * Q)                            # ⟨P̃, Q̃⟩

    return h(A, B) / ops.sqrt(h(A, A) * h(B, B) + 1e-12)


class FairProbNet(keras.Model):
    """The Note-06 probabilistic net + one CKA penalty on its center μ.

    The body is the recipe's MLP with a Gaussian head [μ, log σ²]; the only addition
    is `add_loss(λ·CKA(μ, S))`.  S arrives as `q` and touches the loss alone — never
    the inputs, so the deployed net predicts from features only.
    """
    def __init__(self, lam: float, seed: int = 0):
        super().__init__()
        keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)                      # reproducible init
        self.h1 = layers.Dense(48, activation="tanh")
        self.h2 = layers.Dense(48, activation="tanh")
        self.head = layers.Dense(2)                            # head = [μ, log σ²]
        self.lam = lam                                         # λ — the fairness weight

    def call(self, inputs, training=False):
        x, s = inputs["x"], inputs["q"]                        # x = features (+proxy);  q = S
        pred = self.head(self.h2(self.h1(x)))                  # the model sees FEATURES ONLY
        if training and self.lam > 0:
            self.add_loss(self.lam * cka_in_graph(pred[:, :1], s))   # λ·CKA(μ, S) — S in the loss only
        return pred
```
:::


The class is the Note-06 network move for move; the three new lines are the `lam`
field, the `cka_in_graph` penalty, and the `add_loss` call.  Everything that made the
band breathe — the two-output head, the Gaussian NLL, the predicted $\sigma(x)$ — is
untouched.

## Toy — The Price of Fairness, Made Visible

Build the leak the same way the fairness lab does.  `datasets.fair_regression` gives a
target that bends with $S$ both linearly and through a curve; we hand the model a clean
feature `x` plus a **proxy** $\text{proxy} = S + 0.3\,\varepsilon$ — correlated with $S$
the way `occupation` carries `sex` — and **drop $S$ itself**.  A plain net leans on the
proxy, so its $\mu$ tracks $S$.

::: {#toy-data .cell execution_count=6}
``` {.python .cell-code}
d = datasets.fair_regression(n=600, seed=0)
x: Float[Array, "n"] = d["x"]                       # legitimate feature (clean of S)
S: Float[Array, "n"] = d["s"]                       # protected attribute — NEVER an input
y: Float[Array, "n"] = d["y"]                       # target (bends with S, linearly + curvily)

rng = np.random.default_rng(1)
proxy: Float[Array, "n"] = S + 0.3 * rng.standard_normal(len(S))   # corr(proxy, S) ≈ 0.96

Xf: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.column_stack([x, proxy]).astype("float32")   # features: x + proxy. NO S.
Sc: Float[Array, "n 1"] = S[:, None].astype("float32")                     # S — handed to the loss as q
Y: Float[Array, "n 1"] = y[:, None].astype("float32")

print(f"n={len(S)}   corr(proxy, S) = {np.corrcoef(proxy, S)[0, 1]:.2f}   (the leak channel)")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
n=600   corr(proxy, S) = 0.96   (the leak channel)
```
:::
:::


Train the **same** `FairProbNet` across a sweep of $\lambda$ — off, mild, strong — on the
identical leaking features.  At each setting read four numbers: the dependence
$\operatorname{CKA}(\mu, S)$, the accuracy (RMSE of $\mu$ against the target), the
predicted width $\hat\sigma$, and the $95\%$ coverage the band actually delivers.

::: {#toy-sweep-compute .cell execution_count=7}
``` {.python .cell-code}
# μ depends on x AND the proxy — to draw a clean μ(S) band, sweep S through the proxy
# channel with the legitimate feature x held at its mean.
s_grid: Float[Array, "g"] = np.linspace(S.min(), S.max(), 200)
X_grid: Float[Array, "g 2"] = np.column_stack(
    [np.full_like(s_grid, x.mean()), s_grid]).astype("float32")   # x = mean, proxy = S-grid
q_grid: Float[Array, "g 1"] = s_grid[:, None].astype("float32")


def fit_fair_prob(lam: float) -> dict:
    """Train the Note-06 net + λ·CKA(μ, S); return diagnostics + a clean μ(S) curve."""
    model = FairProbNet(lam, seed=0)
    model.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss=gaussian_nll)
    model.fit({"x": Xf, "q": Sc}, Y, epochs=150, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

    pred: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.asarray(model.predict({"x": Xf, "q": Sc}, verbose=0))
    mu: Float[Array, "n"] = pred[:, 0]                          # μ(x) — the center
    sigma: Float[Array, "n"] = np.exp(0.5 * pred[:, 1])         # σ(x) = exp(½·log σ²)

    grid: Float[Array, "g 2"] = np.asarray(model.predict({"x": X_grid, "q": q_grid}, verbose=0))
    return {
        "mu": mu,
        "sigma": sigma,
        "grid_mu": grid[:, 0],                                  # smooth μ over the S-grid
        "grid_sig": np.exp(0.5 * grid[:, 1]),                   # smooth σ over the S-grid
        "cka": cka_rbf(mu, S),                                  # dependence on S
        "rmse": float(np.sqrt(np.mean((mu - y) ** 2))),         # accuracy cost
        "sigma_hat": float(sigma.mean()),                      # mean predicted width
        "cov95": float(np.mean(np.abs(y - mu) <= 1.96 * sigma)),  # 95% band coverage
    }


sweep = [0.0, 2.0, 8.0]
runs = {lam: fit_fair_prob(lam) for lam in sweep}

print(f"{'λ':>5}  {'CKA(μ,S)':>9}  {'RMSE':>6}  {'σ̂':>6}  {'95% cov':>8}")
print("-" * 42)
for lam in sweep:
    r = runs[lam]
    note = "  ← unfair, tight band" if lam == 0 else ("  ← fair, band widened" if lam == sweep[-1] else "")
    print(f"{lam:>5g}  {r['cka']:>9.3f}  {r['rmse']:>6.2f}  {r['sigma_hat']:>6.2f}  {r['cov95']:>8.2f}{note}")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
    λ   CKA(μ,S)    RMSE      σ̂   95% cov
------------------------------------------
    0      0.256    0.63    0.52      0.96  ← unfair, tight band
    2      0.028    1.25    0.73      0.95
    8      0.006    1.31    0.89      0.96  ← fair, band widened
```
:::
:::


Read the table top to bottom and the whole note is in it.  As $\lambda$ rises,
$\operatorname{CKA}(\mu, S)$ collapses toward zero — the prediction becomes
**independent of $S$**.  RMSE rises — that is the **accuracy cost** of giving up the
$S$-signal.  And $\hat\sigma$ **grows** in step, so the $95\%$ coverage stays put: the
probabilistic net, denied the signal, does not pretend — it **widens its band** and
stays honest.

::: {#cell-fig-toy-bands .cell execution_count=8}
``` {.python .cell-code}
fig, (axL, axR) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(11.5, 4.2), sharey=True)
for ax, lam, col in [(axL, 0.0, COOL), (axR, 8.0, GREEN)]:
    r = runs[lam]
    ax.fill_between(s_grid, r["grid_mu"] - 1.96 * r["grid_sig"], r["grid_mu"] + 1.96 * r["grid_sig"],
                    color=col, alpha=0.30, label="μ ± 2σ̂(x)")
    ax.scatter(S, y, s=10, c=INK, alpha=0.30, edgecolors="none", label="data")
    ax.plot(s_grid, r["grid_mu"], c=INK, lw=2, label="μ(x)")
    tag = "plain (λ=0)" if lam == 0 else "CKA penalty (λ=8)"
    ax.set_title(f"{tag} · CKA(μ,S)={r['cka']:.2f} · σ̂={r['sigma_hat']:.2f} · cov={r['cov95']:.0%}",
                 fontsize=10.5)
    ax.set_xlabel("protected attribute  S")
    despine(ax)

axL.set_ylabel("prediction  μ ± band")
axL.legend(fontsize=9, frameon=False, loc="upper center")
fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

The left band tracks $S$ — accurate but unfair.  The right band is **flat in $S$** —
fair — and *wider*, the net admitting through $\sigma(x)$ that it is now less certain.
Coverage stays near $95\%$ in both panels.  A point net forced to be fair would simply
be more wrong, silently; the probabilistic recipe converts that silence into an honest,
calibrated width.  **That is the deliverable: fairness has a price, and the band quotes
it.**

## The Recipe Carries Over

Nothing above was special to the Gaussian head.  The CKA penalty constrains $\mu(x)$;
*which* uncertainty recipe produces $\mu$ — the Gaussian head, the Student-t head, or a
deep ensemble of either — is orthogonal.  Swap the likelihood and the penalty rides
along unchanged.  The Student-t head from Note 06 takes it verbatim:

::: {#student-carryover-compute .cell execution_count=9}
``` {.python .cell-code}
NU = 4.0                                          # ν = degrees of freedom (heavy tails)


def student_t_nll(y_true, y_pred):
    """−log t_ν(y; μ, σ) up to a constant,  ν=4,  head = [μ, log σ²]  (verbatim from Note 06)."""
    mu = y_pred[:, :1]                            # μ(x)
    log_sig = 0.5 * y_pred[:, 1:2]                # log σ(x) = ½·log σ²

    z = (y_true - mu) / ops.exp(log_sig)          # standardized residual z = (y−μ)/σ

    return ops.mean(log_sig + 0.5 * (NU + 1.0) * ops.log(1.0 + z ** 2 / NU))


stud = FairProbNet(8.0, seed=0)                   # the SAME class — only the loss differs
stud.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.01), loss=student_t_nll)
stud.fit({"x": Xf, "q": Sc}, Y, epochs=150, batch_size=128, verbose=0)

pred_t: Float[Array, "n 2"] = np.asarray(stud.predict({"x": Xf, "q": Sc}, verbose=0))
mu_t: Float[Array, "n"] = pred_t[:, 0]

print(f"Student-t head + λ·CKA(μ, S):  CKA(μ,S) = {cka_rbf(mu_t, S):.3f}   ← penalty fair on the t head too")
print(f"(compare Gaussian head, λ=8:   CKA(μ,S) = {runs[8.0]['cka']:.3f})")
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}
```
Student-t head + λ·CKA(μ, S):  CKA(μ,S) = 0.006   ← penalty fair on the t head too
(compare Gaussian head, λ=8:   CKA(μ,S) = 0.006)
```
:::
:::


The penalty drives the t-head's $\operatorname{CKA}(\mu, S)$ to zero just as it did the
Gaussian head's — same one new term, a different likelihood underneath.  The deep
**ensemble** is the same story one level up: train $M$ fair members, each a
`FairProbNet` with the penalty, and the committee's spread still reports epistemic
doubt — fairness and the uncertainty recipe compose freely.  We use exactly that
ensemble on the real data next.

## Real Example — Income Predictions That Leak Sex

The toy showed the mechanism; here is the stake.  We predict whether a person earns
**over \$50k** from US-Census features — age, education, hours, occupation — the kind
of screening model a bank or lender might actually deploy.  The fairness requirement
is concrete: the prediction must not depend on **sex**.  The obvious fix — drop `sex`
from the inputs — is *not enough*, and that is exactly what makes the problem hard:
`occupation` and `marital` status are **proxies** that let the network reconstruct
sex and reproduce the real-world income gap through the back door.  We need the CKA
penalty to sever that leak, and the probabilistic ensemble to quote what the
neutrality costs.

Now the real panel, with the full recipe: a **deep ensemble of probabilistic
classifiers**, each carrying the CKA penalty.  We **reload** the prepared US-Census
income data — the ACS decode, the `income_high` target, and the protected `sex` are
built once in [The Income & Fairness Dataset](../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd) — split
it into $(X, y, s)$ with `sex` **dropped**.  Even gone, `occupation` leaks it.  The one
local step is one-hot encoding the categoricals, since the model needs numbers:

::: {#real-load .cell execution_count=10}
``` {.python .cell-code}
credit = datasets.load_credit()
y_r: Float[Array, "n"] = credit["income_high"].to_numpy().astype(float)   # target: 1 if income > $50k
s_r: Float[Array, "n"] = credit["sex"].to_numpy().astype(float)           # protected: 1 = male
X_r = credit.drop(columns=["income_high", "sex"])      # proxies — sex DROPPED

# the only local step: one-hot the categoricals, then standardize for the fit
X_enc = pd.get_dummies(X_r, columns=["occupation", "marital"], drop_first=True).to_numpy().astype(float)
X_z: Float[Array, "n d"] = ((X_enc - X_enc.mean(0)) / (X_enc.std(0) + 1e-9)).astype("float32")   # z-score
s_col: Float[Array, "n 1"] = s_r[:, None].astype("float32")
y_col: Float[Array, "n 1"] = y_r[:, None].astype("float32")

print(f"{len(credit):,} rows · X columns (sex dropped): {list(X_r.columns)}")
print(f"encoded proxy matrix: {X_z.shape}")
```

## Where This Data Comes From
The ACS decode, the `income_high` target, the protected `sex` attribute, and the proxy
leak through `occupation` are built and owned **once** in
[The Income & Fairness Dataset](../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd).  This note reloads
that prepared `(X, y, s)` and never re-derives it; the only local step is one-hot
encoding the categoricals, as that page's contract allows.
:::

The members are probabilistic classifiers — each outputs $P(\text{high income})$, and
the **spread across the committee is the epistemic uncertainty**, exactly the Note-06
ensemble move.  The penalty acts on each member's probability, so the committee's center
is driven independent of `sex`.  CKA builds an $n\times n$ gram, so we read dependence on
a ~2000-row subsample; the group gap is read on the full panel:

::: {#real-ensemble-compute .cell execution_count=11}
``` {.python .cell-code}
class FairProbClf(keras.Model):
    """One probabilistic classifier member: P(high income) + λ·CKA(P, sex).

    Same shape as `FairProbNet` — a body, a head, and the one CKA penalty — only the
    head is a sigmoid P(·) and the loss is cross-entropy.  `cka_in_graph` is reused
    unchanged: gradients flow through the probability output just as through μ.
    """
    def __init__(self, lam: float, seed: int):
        super().__init__()
        keras.utils.set_random_seed(seed)
        self.h1 = layers.Dense(32, activation="tanh")
        self.h2 = layers.Dense(16, activation="tanh")
        self.out = layers.Dense(1, activation="sigmoid")        # P(high income | proxies)
        self.lam = lam

    def call(self, inputs, training=False):
        x, s = inputs["x"], inputs["q"]                         # x = proxies;  q = sex
        p = self.out(self.h2(self.h1(x)))                       # the model sees PROXIES ONLY
        if training and self.lam > 0:
            self.add_loss(self.lam * cka_in_graph(p, s))        # λ·CKA(P, sex) — sex in the loss only
        return p


M = 3                                                          # committee size (deep ensemble)
N_FIT = 2000                                                   # rows each member trains on (modest, for speed)
rng_e = np.random.default_rng(0)
idx: Float[Array, "k"] = rng_e.choice(len(y_r), 2000, replace=False)   # subsample for the O(n²) CKA


def train_ensemble(lam: float) -> Float[Array, "m n"]:
    """M fair probabilistic classifiers on bootstrap resamples; stack their P(·) on the full panel."""
    preds = []
    for seed in range(M):
        boot: Float[Array, "f"] = rng_e.integers(0, len(y_r), N_FIT)   # bootstrap resample (subset, for speed)
        clf = FairProbClf(lam, seed=seed)
        clf.compile(optimizer=keras.optimizers.Adam(0.005), loss="binary_crossentropy")
        clf.fit({"x": X_z[boot], "q": s_col[boot]}, y_col[boot],
                epochs=30, batch_size=256, verbose=0)            # minibatch SGD — CKA gram is batch², not n²
        preds.append(np.asarray(clf.predict({"x": X_z, "q": s_col}, verbose=0))[:, 0])   # predict on ALL rows
    return np.stack(preds)


def group_gap(p: Float[Array, "n"]) -> float:
    """Demographic-parity gap: mean prediction for men − for women."""
    return float(p[s_r == 1].mean() - p[s_r == 0].mean())     # P̄(male) − P̄(female)


ens = {lam: train_ensemble(lam) for lam in (0.0, 8.0)}

print(f"{'':18}{'accuracy':>9}  {'group gap':>10}  {'CKA(P,sex)':>11}  {'epistemic σ':>12}")
print("-" * 66)
results = {}
for lam in (0.0, 8.0):
    P: Float[Array, "m n"] = ens[lam]
    p_bar: Float[Array, "n"] = einx.mean("m n -> n", P)        # committee center = mean_m P_m
    sigma_epi: Float[Array, "n"] = np.sqrt(einx.var("m n -> n", P))   # epistemic σ = spread of members
    acc = float(((p_bar > 0.5).astype(int) == y_r).mean())
    results[lam] = (p_bar, sigma_epi, acc)
    tag = "plain (λ=0)" if lam == 0 else "CKA penalty (λ=8)"
    print(f"{tag:18}{acc:>9.3f}  {group_gap(p_bar):>+10.3f}  {cka_rbf(p_bar[idx], s_r[idx]):>11.3f}  {sigma_epi.mean():>12.3f}")
```

The same one new term that erased a toy curve now shrinks a **real** group gap.  The
plain ensemble carries a sizeable parity gap — the very gap the
[primer documents](../data/06-the-credit-dataset.qmd), surviving even with `sex` dropped
because `occupation` leaks it — and CKA detects that the committee center depends on sex.
Add $\lambda\cdot\operatorname{CKA}(P, \text{sex})$ and the dependence falls toward zero,
the two group distributions align, the gap closes — at a few points of accuracy — and the
ensemble still reports its honest epistemic spread.  The probabilistic recipe survived
the constraint intact.

## Close

The dependence machinery never changed.  CKA — built on the double-centering of the
distance-correlation ladder — *measured* dependence between return series in the
[dependence chapter](../dependence/index.qmd); here the same bounded measure
**constrained the probabilistic network**, forcing its prediction independent of a
protected attribute with one extra loss term.  And because the net was the Note-06
probabilistic recipe, the price of that fairness did not vanish into a quietly-wronger
point estimate — it surfaced as a **wider, still-calibrated band**.  Measure and
constrain are one operation read in two directions.

The finance twin is immediate: a prediction forced **independent of a protected
attribute** is the same construction as a portfolio forced **market-neutral** or
**beta-neutral** — strip out the factor you are not allowed to bet on, and price what the
neutrality costs.  For the full treatment — the drop-and-leak failure, the end-to-end
neutralisation, and the accuracy–fairness frontier — see the
[fair learning chapter](../fairness/index.qmd).
